topic_rules: DATA CAVEAT FIRST: ep01 got 43 views, but only about 20 came from impressions (862 x 1.97% = ~17 Suggested, 34 x 8.82% = 3 Browse, 0 Search). The other ~23 came from links, the channel page or direct visits. About 19 of the views were on phones. Trust the direction of every finding below, not its decimals. The Browse CTR of 8.82% rests on 3 clicks and may be the owner's own circle, so it does not prove the thumbnail works.

T1. Pick a concrete subject you can picture from 3 words: one named place, object or event (a specific lake, bay, island, flood, wreck or town). Ep01's subject was an abstract pattern spread across 7 landmasses ('continents point south'), and neither a thumbnail nor a phone screen can show that at a glance.

T2. The core payoff must be something you SEE change or appear, rendered photoreal by our engine: drain the water to show the floor (DEM seafloor), remove the ice, compare a coastline before and after, lay a true-size overlay, or fly into a place nobody can visit. An argument is not a payoff. Ep01's payoff (a Gondwana breakup explains the tips) was a chain of reasoning. Its one praised moment, the antipode overlay at 2:40-3:05, was a spatial reveal. Choose a topic whose story naturally contains 5-7 such reveals.

T3. The topic needs one clear, true answer that fits in a single sentence, with no hedging. Ep01's answer was 'They're not [a coincidence]. Not entirely.' A hedged truth leaves only weak packaging or clickbait. Reject topics whose honest answer is 'partly' or 'scientists still debate it'. Use a myth-busting frame only when the myth is widely believed and the correction is crisp; otherwise frame the video as a true story or a reveal.

T4. Give the film a human story spine with stakes: one event or protagonist, a timeline with a turning point, and real consequences (lives, money, a mistake, a survival). Use at most 3 named people in the whole film. Ep01 was the history of an idea (Bacon, Forster, Humboldt/Guyot, Green, Wegener, a magazine writer, a geologist) with no single protagonist, and the idea-history chapter is exactly where phone viewers left (they averaged 2:11, and chapter 1 ran to 2:15).

T5. The topic must show demand on both surfaces a new channel depends on (98% of ep01 viewers were non-subscribers, and 93% of impressions came from Suggested). (a) Search: the core phrase has real volume, roughly 50K or more estimated monthly searches, or a strongly rising keyword. Ep01 got 9 search impressions and 0 clicks. (b) Suggested 'host' videos: at least 3 existing videos on the same place or premise with 500K+ views, and at least one of them under 3 months old and still gaining (300+ views/hour, like the drain / without-ice / forbidden-island outliers). Our Suggested impressions come from sitting next to those hosts. Ep01 had no active host cluster, so YouTube tested it beside videos whose viewers did not want it (1.97% CTR).

T6. The angle must not be saturated. Reject the topic if 2 or more recent, well-made long-form videos with over 1M views already tell the same story from the same angle (check with the ytsearch probe). Aim for a proven premise applied to an untold place or angle.

T7. Give it a US anchor. The US was 28% of views but 43% of watch time, so US viewers watched about 1.9x longer than everyone else (43/28 vs 57/72). Prefer a US place, US stakes or a subject Americans know, and use US-familiar scale comparisons (miles, feet, football fields, Texas). It must still make sense to a global audience.

T8. Keep the geography phone-sized: the subject must work at regional zoom and fill at least a third of the frame. Avoid topics whose point needs the whole globe, or many small features on screen at once. Ep01 needed Greenland, Florida, Baja, Kamchatka and India on one globe, and each was a few millimetres wide on a phone.

T9. Pick a topic that gives viewers something to comment on: a personal stake or an opinion (have you been there, would you go, who was to blame, what would you have done). Ep01 got 0 comments and 0 shares.
packaging_rules: P1. Design for the Suggested feed on a phone first, because 93% of ep01's impressions were Suggested, at 1.97% CTR. Before upload, mock the package in DARK MODE at two sizes: the full-width phone card (about 390x220 pt) and the compact list/sidebar card (about 168x94 px). Place it beside the 5 strongest host-video thumbnails. If ours is not the most readable and brightest card in that strip, redo it.

P2. Title: 35-50 characters (ep01 had 55; the niche outlier median is 51; past about 45 characters, compact cards start to cut it off). Put the proper noun in the first 3 words, include one concrete noun the viewer can picture, and use no hedge words ('Not Just', 'Sort Of', 'Maybe', 'Kind Of'). Ep01, 'Why the Continents Point South (Not Just a Coincidence)', spent its bracket on a hedge instead of a cancelled obvious answer.

P3. Use the exact place or event words that the host videos and searchers use, so YouTube's content matching can place us next to them and Search can surface us. Then add our twist. Name the subject in the first spoken sentence and in the first line of the description too, because the transcript also feeds the matching.

P4. The curiosity gap must be a specific withheld thing the viewer already wants to know (what is at the bottom, why nobody may land there, what happened to the people). It must not be an abstract question the viewer did not have before seeing the card; ep01's 'POINTING AT WHAT?' needed the viewer to care about a pattern first. A statement that withholds one detail beats a vague why/what question.

P5. Thumbnail composition: one focal subject filling at least 50% of the frame. Use 0-3 words of text, each line at least 20% of the thumbnail's height, white on a black box with one accent-colour word. Use at most ONE graphic device (one arrow OR one ring). At least 40% of the area should be bright or saturated, never a navy-dominated background, which blends into dark-mode YouTube. Ep01's thumbnail had about 5 competing elements (3 orange continents, 3 arrows, a ring, a '?' and 3 words of text) on a dark navy map.

P6. The thumbnail image creates the gap by showing the BEFORE or PARTIAL state of the hero reveal: a half-drained basin, a shape under the water, a forbidden shore with one marker. The text adds emotion or stakes and never repeats the title.

P7. Frame 1 of the video is the thumbnail image in motion (keep this from ep01). The video delivers part of the thumbnail's promise on screen within 30 s and all of it by the end. That confirms the click and protects watch time and satisfaction.

P8. Targets: Suggested CTR of 5% or more (2.5x ep01) and overall CTR of 5% or more. Measure watch time per impression (CTR x average view duration): ep01 got about 5.2 s (2.27% x 231 s). The ep02 target is 15 s or more, about 3x.

P9. Upload 3 thumbnails to Test & Compare, but do not read the result before roughly 10K impressions. At ep01's 925 impressions, a 2% versus 3% difference is noise. Choose the default thumbnail with the mock-feed test in P1, not by gut.
hook_rules: H1. 0:00-0:03: frame 1 is the thumbnail in motion. The first spoken line names the subject and the stakes in 12 words or fewer. No logo, no title card, no intro sting.

H2. The first 10 s must work with the sound off. Home-feed inline playback on phones starts muted with captions, and viewers who arrive by autoplay from Suggested never chose the video. Use motion plus ONE big label, and upload accurate captions.
H3. By 0:15, state the single central question in the same words as the title or thumbnail, to confirm the click.

H4. By 0:30, show the first hero shot: the best photoreal spatial reveal in the film, including a partial view of the thumbnail payoff. Ep01's best shot, the antipode overlay, came at 2:40, after the average phone viewer had already left at 2:11.
H5. By 0:45-0:60, start the actual story at a specific person, place and moment. Open in the middle of the action if possible, then rewind.

H6. No menu or table of contents. Never use 'along the way', 'by the end you'll know' or a list of upcoming topics (ep01 did this at 0:37-0:54 with 'dig to China, an 1875 theory, future collisions'). Allow at most ONE forward promise, and it must be the story's own question.
H7. No historical asides, quotes, Latin, static portraits or 'history of the idea' dates in the first 2 minutes. Ep01's Bacon Latin quote over a static portrait (1:00-1:25) is the example to avoid.

H8. Density cap for 0:00-1:00: no more than 2 named people, 1 date and 1 number, with sentences of 15 words or fewer. Ep01's first chapter as aired (0:00-2:15) packed roughly 5 named people or sources, 5 dates or eras, 2 statistics and a 3-item menu, and phone viewers averaged 2:11.
H9. No hedging in the hook (ep01 said 'They're not. Not entirely.'). Commit to the true, clear claim.
H10. Something moves every second, and the camera is close (regional view). Never open on a slow whole-globe drift.

H11. Retention targets: 70% or more still watching at 0:30, 60% or more at 1:00, and mobile average view duration of 30% or more (ep01: 14.1%). The 0:30 and 1:00 figures are niche rules of thumb, not from our own data.
pacing_rules: C1. Cut cadence: ep01 averaged 10.75 s between hard cuts (93 cuts in 1,011 s). Ep02 target: a hard cut or a new visual event every 3-5 s, an average shot length of 5 s or less, and never more than 6 s without a new element. Ep01's QC flagged 25 near-static stretches longer than 3.5 s.
C2. Camera moves: point-to-point flights take 1.5-3 s with easing. Use slow drifts only underneath an overlay that is changing. 'Slow globe moves' were one of ep01's named phone problems.

C3. Text size for phones: in portrait, the 1920 px frame shrinks to about 390 pt (x0.2). Set labels at 64 px or larger at 1080p (about 13 pt on the phone) and key words at 90-120 px. Lines, arrows, borders and arcs that matter must be 8-10 px or thicker. Show at most 3 labels at once, and keep text out of the bottom 20% (captions) and the top 8%.
C4. Subject size: whatever the narration names must fill at least a third of the frame's width at that moment. Whole-globe shots last 3 s or less and take no more than 10% of the runtime.

C5. Idea budget: at most 2 new ideas per minute, at most 1 new named person per chapter (3 in the whole film), at most 1 spoken number per minute, and at most 5 big on-screen numbers in the whole film (owner rule: only a few big vivid numbers). Each number appears as a counter at least a quarter of the frame tall. Every idea is shown on screen, not only said.
C6. Narration: 150-160 words per minute and sentences of 15 words or fewer. Quotes stay under 10 words and appear only when the picture shows the action, never over a portrait.

C7. Re-hook every 60-90 s with a reveal, a change of location, an in-world gag or a new open question. Each chapter tops the one before it in stakes or spectacle. Ep01 peaked at 2:40, then slid into a history of ideas.

C8. Chapters: 5-6 chapters of 2-3 minutes each (ep01 had 9, averaging 1:44, the shortest 63 s). Chapter 1 is the hook and lasts 1:30 or less. Chapter titles tease in the story's own words: never the answer, never 'Intro' or 'Conclusion'. Each chapter = one sub-question + one hero shot + one mini-reveal + a last line that opens the next question.

C9. Payoff placement: the full answer to the thumbnail question lands at 85-90% of the runtime. Ep01 answered its core question at 9:13-10:43 (59-69% of the runtime), then ran about 4:50 of extra sections (the joke, what doesn't drip, future supercontinents).

C10. No call to action inside the story: no subscribe, like, 'Juice Check' or comment prompt before the final line. Ep01's 4:57-5:07 subscribe break interrupted the flow just before its strongest reveal. A recurring branded beat is allowed only if it is a story beat, not an ask.

C11. Humour: in-world visual gags of 3-6 s every 2-3 minutes, using characters on the real terrain and keeping the story moving. Funny lines in the script (like ep01's 'left the planet on the dashboard in July') stay, but each one gets a visual.
visual_rules: V1. One visual language for the whole film: a photoreal real-Earth base (the Blue Marble/VIIRS globe, DEM terrain and seafloor, NASA GIBS satellite patches), with one colour grade, one font, one accent-colour system and one label style from first frame to last.

V2. The CC0 low-poly characters appear only inside the photoreal scenes. They stand on the real terrain with matched lighting, shadows and believable scale, like figures on a relief model, never in a separate stylised set. Ep01's stylised corridor scene (7:35-7:50) clashed with the globe look. If a beat needs a set we cannot build photoreal, cut it or stage it on the terrain.
V3. Public-domain archival photos: 4 s or less each, always moving (Ken Burns), with the same frame treatment, and no more than 1 per minute. Never cover an aside with a static portrait.

V4. Build the film around the thing viewers loved: spatial overlays on the real 3D Earth that make an invisible relationship visible. The antipode overlay at 2:40-3:05 was called 'remarkably vivid and professional'. Plan 5-7 such hero shots: the first by 0:30, then one per chapter (about every 2 minutes), with the payoff as the last. The engine's natural hero shots are draining the water (DEM seafloor), true-size overlays, before/after coastlines, cut-aways and flights into places nobody can visit.

V5. Frame for the phone: use regional camera altitudes and keep the subject at least a third of the frame. Dim and desaturate the surroundings and colour the subject with a single accent (ep01's subject-highlight approach was right). Avoid dense maps with many borders, rivers and labels on screen at once.
V6. Give each moment one focal point. Do not stack a drift, a morph, labels and arcs at the same time; one thing moves meaningfully while the rest supports it.
V7. Keep the thumbnail, frame 1 and the payoff shot continuous: the same subject, the same accent colour and the same camera angle family, so the film visibly keeps the thumbnail's promise.
ending_rules: E1. The payoff is the last story beat. The final line answers the thumbnail question in one sentence over the final hero shot. No recap, no stacked closers and no speculative coda after the answer; ep01 put a recap and the future-supercontinent section after its answer.

E2. Within 0-3 s after the final line, give a one-sentence spoken hand-off to ONE specific next video on a related theme. Phrase it as a new question; if ep02 is a water or drain story, the channel's Lake Peigneur film is the natural pick. The aim is to keep the viewer watching our channel.

E3. The end-screen elements (YouTube's 5-20 s window) sit over a last shot that is still moving, never an empty or black frame. The whole end screen lasts 15 s or less, and the video cuts about 1 s after the hand-off line. Ep01's end cards came too early, over an empty frame.
E4. End-screen layout: the one specific next video, plus the subscribe element. The 'best for viewer' slot is secondary.

E5. At most one short subscribe line, folded into the hand-off and never before the payoff; leaving it out entirely is fine. The comment prompt lives in the pinned comment and in at most one closing sentence. Tie it to the story with an opinion or 'what would you do' question, not a generic ask (ep01: 0 comments).
lessons.target_length: 12:30-14:00, aiming for 13:00 (about 1,950-2,100 words at ~155 wpm), with a hard ceiling of 15:00 and the payoff at about 11:15-11:45. The reasoning: (1) Length was not what drove phone viewers away. They left at an average of 2:11, inside chapter 1, which points at the opening and its density, not the 15:34 runtime. Meanwhile desktop (7:53, 50.7%) and TV (8:24, 54.1%) viewers, the biggest share of US watch time, stayed for half of a 15-minute film. Going very short (around 10 minutes) would therefore give up watch time from the viewers who already liked the film. (2) Ep01 still carried dead weight: 77 s had to be cut in post, and about 4:50 came after the core answer. Its strong material was roughly 10-11 minutes. A 13-minute film with the answer at 85-90% of the runtime removes that tail. (3) The numbers: a 42% average view duration on 13:00 is 5:28 (ep01: 3:51), and 30% on phones is 3:54 (ep01: 2:11). At 5% CTR that gives about 16 s of watch time per impression, roughly 3x ep01's 5.2 s. (4) In the outlier pull, the spectacle formats won at 11-12 minutes (Antarctica without ice 11:21, all ice melted 11:58) and the story or forbidden-place formats at about 20-22 minutes (Iwo Jima 20:02, the Contour Atlas drains). 13 minutes sits between the two, inside the 10-18 minute rule. A story-heavy topic may run to 15 minutes only if each extra minute carries its own hero shot. (5) Staying above 8 minutes keeps mid-roll ads possible once the channel is monetized. (6) Production does not limit length: Colab renders about a minute of film per minute. The real limit is having 5-7 hero shots at roughly one every 2 minutes.
lessons.topic_vs_execution:
VERDICT: ep01's reach problem (CTR and Search) was mainly a TOPIC problem. Its phone-retention problem was mainly an EXECUTION problem, made worse by the topic. Topic is the bigger lever, because CTR decides how many impressions YouTube will ever test: ep01 got 925 in 35 hours, then stalled.

TOPIC PROBLEMS:
(1) Search demand was close to zero: 9 search impressions, 0 clicks. Nothing in execution could fix that.
(2) Most of the 1.97% Suggested CTR. The premise is an abstract pattern across 7 landmasses with a hedged true answer ('not entirely a coincidence'), and no active cluster of host videos existed. YouTube placed it next to videos whose viewers did not want it, and no thumbnail can sell an abstract, hedged premise to a viewer who is mid-video on something else.
(3) The structure was a history of an idea (a chain of thinkers from 1620 to the 1970s) rather than one event with a protagonist and stakes. That structure came from the topic, and it is where phone viewers left.
(4) The whole-globe scale made phone legibility hard by nature: many small features had to be on screen at once.
(5) No personal stake for viewers: 0 comments, 0 shares.

EXECUTION PROBLEMS (all fixable regardless of topic):
- A menu hook at 0:37-0:54.
- A Bacon static-portrait aside at 1:00-1:25.
- The best shot buried at 2:40, after the average phone viewer had left (2:11).
- A 'Juice Check / Subscribe' break mid-story at 4:57-5:07.
- A clashing stylised corridor scene at 7:35-7:50.
- About 10.75 s between cuts, 25 near-static stretches, small labels, dense maps and slow globe moves.
- The payoff at 59-69% of the runtime, followed by about 5 minutes of extra sections.
- End cards that came early, over an empty frame.
- A busy, dark thumbnail with about 5 competing elements, and a title bracket spent on a hedge.

NOT THE PROBLEM:
- The narration quality, the photoreal look and the 3D-overlay craft. A 50.7% average view duration on computers and 54.1% on TV for a 15:34 film shows the core craft holds attention on a big screen. The US (43% of watch time from 28% of views) was the audience that stayed.

MIXED:
- Phone retention of 14.1%: roughly half execution (opening, density, text size, cut pace) and half topic (abstract, global scale, no story spine).

SAMPLE-SIZE CAVEAT:
- About 20 algorithm-driven clicks and about 19 phone views. The directions are consistent with YouTube's own retention critique, but the exact percentages are noisy.

- All Studio numbers and critique timestamps come from the context file.

shortlist.working_title: We Drained Lake Powell Down to Dead Pool
shortlist.premise: Lake Powell, America's second-largest reservoir, hit a record low in August 2026, then jumped about 12-16 ft in October storms. We remove the rest of the water using the USGS topobathymetric model (2017 multibeam, 2018 lidar and pre-dam surveys), and the drowned Glen Canyon comes back: side canyons, the Cathedral in the Desert, stranded marinas, the power-pool and dead-pool lines, and a mud delta over 100 ft thick creeping toward the dam. The dam itself is the human story: in 1983 it nearly tore itself apart from too much water, and in 2026 it came within about 30 ft of losing power from too little.
shortlist.story_spine: COLD OPEN, June 1983: the dam's spillway tunnel coughs red sandstone and concrete into the river, and crews bolt plywood, then steel boards, onto the gates to hold the lake back. 'In 1983 this lake nearly broke the dam. In 2026 it nearly ran dry.' HERO SHOT BY 0:30: the water plane drops 100 ft in one move and canyon walls appear. CH2: the canyon nobody knew before 1963 (at most 2 names: Brower, who traded it away and regretted it, and Dominy, who built the dam). CH3, drain step 1: full pool, and the 1983 cavitation crisis shown as a cut-away of the tunnel. CH4: the record low of 3,519.91 ft strands Hite Marina, and the Cathedral in the Desert re-emerges. CH5: 3,490 ft, the turbines stop; 3,370 ft, dead pool, and the river can no longer pass the dam. TWIST (about 85% in): the lake is filling from the bottom, with sediment deltas taking roughly 7% of capacity since 1963, and the October flood brought more. PAYOFF: the full drain down to the mud and bedrock, the dam standing in front of a canyon it can no longer fill. One-sentence answer: under Lake Powell is a drowned canyon, and the lake is slowly turning into mud. Hand-off: Lake Peigneur.
shortlist.hero_image: Glen Canyon Dam with the lake half-drained: the top half of the curved concrete face bare and pale, the turquoise water far below, red drowned-canyon walls exposed, and one tiny houseboat sitting on dry slickrock. Bright red and turquoise, no navy. 2-3 words max, e.g. 'DEAD POOL'.
shortlist.archetype: Drain / 'what's hidden at the bottom', our most proven outlier format: Contour Atlas Chesapeake 170K in 1 week and Great Lakes 165K on 1.4K subs; 'Antarctica Without Ice' 1.8M on 2.9K subs. It lands on a hot US subject: 'lake powell' is a rising keyword (~163K/mo, +150%, US). Active same-place hosts: Eric Hanson 1.95M (4 months) and 799K (2 months), KSL 'Record jump in water levels' 780K in 10 days, Desert Rat 3.4M (per ideator), Explorer Vault 314K (1 month). My probe found no drain-format video of Lake Powell.

shortlist.why: The best overall fit to the lessons. It is a concrete US place (T1, T7). The drain ladder gives 5-7 natural on-screen reveals at regional, phone-sized zoom (T2, T8, V4). The true answer fits in one sentence (T3), and water politics plus 'have you boated it?' give viewers something to comment on (T9). Demand shows on both surfaces: a rising US keyword and several active same-place hosts under 3 months old with 500K+ views (T5). The drain angle is unclaimed (T6). Weaknesses: the protagonist is the dam, not a person (T4), so the 1983 crisis must carry the human stakes. The niche is cluttered with 'RISING/DYING' clickbait, so the packaging must lead with the drained-canyon image. Keep the advocacy out (Eric Hanson owns the 'dam was a mistake' essay). Before scripting, re-verify the 2026 levels and the 1983 peak elevation.

shortlist.working_title: The Year California Became a 300-Mile Lake
shortlist.premise: In the winter of 1861-62 storms hit California for about 43 days, and the Central Valley filled into a brown inland sea about 250-300 miles long, roughly the length of Lake Michigan. Sacramento drowned. By most accounts the new governor went to his inauguration by rowboat, and the legislature fled to San Francisco. The city later jacked its downtown streets up a full storey. Sediment cores show floods like this recur every century or two, and in 2023 the vanished Tulare Lake came back on farmland to prove it.
shortlist.story_spine: COLD OPEN, January 1862: a rowboat glides down a Sacramento street past second-floor windows. HERO SHOT BY 0:30: the real Central Valley DEM floods from the south and north until one long lake fills California. CH2: the witness, geologist William Brewer, whose letters describe water from the Coast Range to the Sierra (named people: Brewer and Stanford, 2 in all). CH3: why the valley is a bathtub, with one narrow drain at Carquinez Strait and the Golden Gate (cut-away). CH4: Sacramento raises itself. A cut-away shows the buried first floors that are still under the city, with a low-poly in-world gag of a city jacking itself up. CH5: the ghost lake. Tulare Lake, once the largest lake west of the Mississippi, was drained for farms, and a GIBS before/after shows it returning in spring 2023. TWIST (about 85% in): the cores show that 1862 was not the biggest; such floods recur. PAYOFF: refill the valley over today's night lights (the USGS ARkStorm scenario), stated without fear-mongering. Final line: California's real Big One has already happened once, and it was water.
shortlist.hero_image: Orbital view of California with the whole Central Valley filled by one long, bright, muddy-brown lake, the Sierra snow-white beside it, and a tiny rowboat in front of a half-submerged capitol dome in the foreground corner.
shortlist.archetype: A 'what if' and drain spectacle run in reverse (we fill the valley), backed by a true disaster: 'What If All the Ice Melted' 961K on 1.5K subs, the Contour Atlas drains. Demand: Tulare Lake Shorts at 22M and 15M, Map Pack 'Why One of USA's Biggest Lakes Is Reappearing' 1.6M, Joe Scott ARkStorm 1.21M. Recent smaller hosts: Paul McAllister 223K (1 month), Waterwake 211K (2 months), Park Vibes 197K (2 months). The 1862 narrative itself has no long-form above about 11K. Rising keywords: 'disasters explained' +110%, 'what would happen if' +134%.
shortlist.why: It has a concrete US subject and a signature reveal the engine does natively (a flood-fill of the real valley) that fills a phone screen (T1, T2, T8). The answer is clear and true (T3). It has a city-in-crisis spine with only 2 names (T4), and Californians will comment (T9). Timing is seasonal: California's atmospheric-river season starts now. Risks: the active hosts are under 500K, so T5(b) needs the deeper check, and two small channels started on 1862 in the last 2-3 months, so the window is closing. The rowboat story must be framed as 'by most accounts', and 'up to 300 miles' should follow Brewer's wording. Avoid a precise death toll and the 'state went bankrupt' claim. Cite one ARkStorm figure source.

shortlist.working_title: Tristan da Cunha Chose the Volcano Over England
shortlist.premise: In October 1961 a volcano opened a few hundred metres behind the only village on Tristan da Cunha, the most remote inhabited island on Earth. All 264 islanders were shipped about 6,000 miles to England and housed at an old RAF camp at Calshot, among buses, escalators, wages and winter flu. In a 1962 ballot they voted 148 to 5 to go back to the volcano, and most did in 1963. The film answers the question every viewer has: why would anyone choose that?
shortlist.story_spine: COLD OPEN (verify): May 2026, RAF paratroopers jump onto an island with no airstrip to reach one sick man. 'That's how hard it is to reach Tristan. Now imagine getting everyone off.' Alternative cold open: 10 Oct 1961, the hill behind the cottages swells and splits. HERO SHOT BY 0:30: pull back from the island until no other land is in frame, then drain the ocean to show Tristan as the tip of a giant seamount. CH2: the eruption, a night among seabirds on Nightingale Island, and a passing Dutch liner picks everyone up. CH3: the arc to Southampton and life at Calshot. The culture shock (escalators, traffic, money) runs as gentle in-world gags; the serious beat is the colds, the flu and the deaths of some elderly islanders. CH4: the 1962 Royal Society expedition finds the village standing. A before/after terrain shot shows the lava stopping short but burying the crayfish factory and both landing beaches. CH5: the ballot, 148 to 5. The return in 1963, and the new harbour named 'Calshot Harbour'. PAYOFF: what they went back for, in their own reported words, and the island today. Named people: Chief Islander Willie Repetto and at most one more. Comment prompt: would you have gone back?
shortlist.hero_image: A tiny row of white cottages at the foot of a huge dark green volcanic cone with a fresh orange lava glow right behind the roofs, open sea on every side, and a small line of people with suitcases walking TOWARD the glow. Text: 'THEY CHOSE THIS'.
shortlist.archetype: A remote / forbidden island riding a live search wave. 'tristan da cunha' is ~315K/mo, +118%. Active same-place hosts: Ruhi Cenet 27.7M (under 1 month), Joe HaTTab 32.1M (7 months), Discovery Destination 5.0M (6 months), Geography By Geoff 4.7M. Premise siblings: 'Why Can't You Visit Iwo Jima?' 4.4M on 3.5K subs, 'Every Forbidden Island' 878K on 1.5K subs. All the big videos are travel or 'life there' angles. My probe today: the 1961 evacuation has 0 long-form videos at 100K+ (the best on-topic is a Royal Society film at 57K, 9 years old), and about 8 recent copies (one 6 days old) all have under 2K views.

shortlist.working_title: Colorado Isn't a Rectangle, and It's the Law

ranked.title: The Dutch Drained a Sea and Found 400 Ships
ranked.angle:
Yes, an angle is clearly unclaimed: "Drain the Oceans, but real." Nat Geo's Drain the Oceans franchise (2-32M views per episode) and Contour Atlas only simulate drains. Here a real sea was really pumped dry, and the film works as a dig down through the seabed's layers. No incumbent asks what was on the bottom.

Proposed structure (reverse-chronology dig):
1. Cold open on the US-anchored find. A US government source says that while the Dutch were pumping one of the polders, "a plane with a U.S. star insignia gradually came into view". It was B-24H 42-7638 "Big Banner" of the 44th Bomb Group, shot down on 22 Dec 1943 with one survivor. The bodies of five crew were found in it during the 1970s recovery, and parts are now in the USAF museum in Dayton.
2. The ships: more than 400 wrecks. The anchor is the English "Queen Anne" merchantman, ca. 1700-1720, near Rutten, with still-filled wine bottles, jars of olives and peaches, and two Queen Anne spoons.
3. The drowned medieval villages: Marcnesse, Nagele and Fenehuysen I and II, found in 2020.
4. The 1945 re-flood as the midpoint twist.
5. A modern ticking clock that nobody uses: the dry land that revealed the ships is now destroying them. Drying, soil settling and ploughing are turning wrecks into "ghost ships", and the Queen Anne's wood was pulverised in a heatwave. Meanwhile the never-drained Markerwaard still holds ships preserved in the mud.
6. Payoff: Almere, 230K people on a 1968 seabed.

ranked.title: Why Nobody Lives on Attu Island Anymore
ranked.angle:
The villagers' trip told as one map journey, ending on the denied homecoming. No incumbent tells it this way.
- Sept 1942: 42 people are taken from America's last village, 1,616 miles to Otaru on Hokkaido.
- About half of them die there.
- 1945: the survivors are freed and sent home across the Pacific through Seattle.
- At the end they are left on Atka, about 530 miles short of their own island. The US government judged rebuilding Attu too costly.
- Payoff: in 2017, 11 descendants finally land at Chichagof Harbor and find only the church foundation. In Nov 2023, Gregory Golodoff, the last survivor, dies. In Dec 2024, the chief's great-granddaughter demands reparations from Japan.

Across The Globe gives this about 5 minutes inside a geography survey, and War Monger's 4K video has no map spectacle. The return journey ("they came home to the wrong island") is the twist that no incumbent uses, and it suits the globe engine: real great-circle arcs, real distances, and an empty village site in 3D terrain.

Two changes to the brief:
1. Make the Kiska armada a 60-90 second dry-irony interlude, not the main twist. Shorts have worn it out.
2. Drop the "forbidden / why can't you visit" frame. Across The Globe already uses it, and it is inaccurate, because Attu can be visited with permits. "Why nobody lives there" is accurate.

The map quirks (Attu is in the Eastern Hemisphere; the date line bends around it; Yank magazine wrongly called Foster Jones the "first Western Hemisphere POW") are already in Across The Globe's description. They still work as a quick hook but are not unclaimed.

ranked.title: Colorado Isn't a Rectangle, and It's the Law
ranked.angle:
Tell it as one story, "the mistake that became the law", with a war of stones as the spine. All four steps below are confirmed in the Supreme Court record (267 U.S. 30 and the 268 U.S. 108 decree).
1. In 1868 Darling sets stones along the 37th parallel.
2. By 1902 an inspector finds that few of the corners still exist and calls the line "evidently erroneously established".
3. The government sends Howard Carpenter to resurvey and specifically tells him to "obliterate" Darling's monuments. Congress accepts Carpenter's line in 1908, and the President vetoes it.
4. In 1925 the Supreme Court says the old line wins, orders Carpenter's corners destroyed and Darling's destroyed corners put back, and appoints a commissioner (Arthur D. Kidder) to re-mark the line. One secondary source says the confusion lasted until 1960.

Nothing on YouTube tells this. Two more beats nobody uses:
- Even a perfectly surveyed Colorado would not be a rectangle. On a globe the north edge is about 21 miles shorter than the south edge (about 365 vs 387 mi). Use this as a 20-second "pedant beat" so the comments do not do it for us.
- Darling himself: born in Vermont in 1832, a Civil War lieutenant in the 18th U.S. Colored Infantry, died in June 1912 (the year New Mexico became a state) leaving an estate worth $23, "a few items of furniture and his compass". He is buried at Arlington. This comes from one secondary source.

The Four Corners "2.5 miles off" media myth of 2009 gives a myth inside the myth: NGS corrected it to about 1,800 ft or less, and said the monument is legally where it should be. That suits the mapmyth lens.

ranked.title: The Coldest Place on Earth Lost Its Power
ranked.angle:
Only partly unclaimed. The premise and its packaging are already taken: Outlier Atlas's title alone combines −128°F, "lost all power" and "refused rescue," and a dozen farms say "20 men survived −70°C."

What nobody does yet is a phone-first, data-led single-clock structure:
- a real temperature dial driven by NOAA's daily Vostok observations. GHCN-Daily holds 113 daily means from Apr–Nov 1982 that this crew kept recording through the blackout; the coldest is −79.2°C on 27 Aug 1982. "The weather reports never stopped" is a true, provable beat no incumbent uses.
- one continuous 3D pull-back and cut-away, from the hut, to the dome of the ice sheet, to the hidden lake about 3.7-4 km below.

That is an execution edge, not a fresh story or premise. Because the 1983 record and the lake are separate facts, the twin "twist" ending is also used loosely by others: "−128°F" already sits in an incumbent title.

finalists.premise: Drain the Pacific around Hawaii step by step, and paradise becomes the tallest mountain on Earth measured from its base (Mauna Kea, about 10,000 m), with city-sized landslide blocks and a chain of older, sinking islands running all the way to Midway. That atoll is an old Hawaiian volcano that has sunk, and the 1942 battle was fought over it, with the carriers from that battle lying in the deep water nearby. Below the Big Island, the next Hawaiian island is already growing underwater.
finalists.story_spine: COLD OPEN, 1 April 1946, Laupahoehoe: the sea suddenly drains off the reef, children run out to look, and it comes back. 'For a few minutes the sea drained away. We're going to finish the job.' HERO SHOT BY 0:30: the first 120 m drop joins Maui, Molokai, Lanai and Kahoolawe into one Ice Age island. The DRAIN LADDER gives one reveal per chapter. At -1,000 m: the Nuuanu slide, where half of an Oahu volcano lies on the seafloor in city-sized blocks. At -5,000 m: the Big Island stands up as one mountain, with an Everest silhouette beside it for scale and its weight bending the seafloor into a moat. Then follow the chain northwest as the islands get older and lower, out to Midway's ring of reef. The Kaga, Akagi and Yorktown wrecks lie in the deep water off it (found 1998 and 2019). TWIST (about 85% in): every island you know is on the same conveyor and will become a Midway. PAYOFF: swing back southeast to Kama'ehuakanaloa growing below the Big Island, then refill the ocean. 'Everything you've seen of Hawaii is the very tip.' Named people: 0-2.

There is a real gap: a Hawaii-only drain built on real bathymetry that turns into a time machine along the chain. No incumbent combines these four things:
1. The drain ladder down to the abyssal floor.
2. The moat reveal. The Big Island is so heavy it has pushed the seafloor down; the Moho is bent down as much as 8 km under Mauna Loa (USGS). Counted from that sunken base, Mauna Loa stands about 17 km tall, almost twice Everest. This beats the Shorts-worn "Mauna Kea is 10 km" fact as a payoff.

Midway can then work as 'a battle fought on the grave of a volcano', with the carrier wrecks revealed when the drain reaches about -5,000 m. No Hawaii or Pacific drain video I found uses that structure.

check.facts_status:
The core story is true and well documented. Several details in the pitch need fixing.

TRUE:
- 1 April 1946 tsunami. It was generated by an Aleutian-trench earthquake (Earth Magazine gives M8.1; other sources give about 8.6), arrived about 5 hours later, and killed 159 people in Hawaii (96 in Hilo). At Laupahoehoe the sea drew back and children went to look at fish flopping on the sand. Earth Magazine says it swept away '16 children and five teachers'; other sources give 24 dead in total, with breakdowns of 20+4 or 21+3. The disaster led to the Pacific Tsunami Warning Center (1948). Sources: https://www.earthmagazine.org/article/benchmarks-april-1-1946-hawaii-tsunami-ushers-pacific-wide-warning-system/ , https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laup%C4%81hoehoe,_Hawaii , https://www.hawaiitribune-herald.com/2021/04/01/hawaii-news/a-wall-of-water-survivors-reflect-on-devastating-tsunami-that-struck-hilo-75-years-ago/
- Nuuanu slide. About half of Ko'olau volcano collapsed, roughly 1 to 1.5 million years ago. The debris runs about 200 km and is called one of the largest landslides on Earth. USGS says the largest block is 'about the size of Manhattan'; the Tuscaloosa block is about 30x20x1.5 km. Moore et al. (USGS 1994) count 68 slides longer than 20 km along the ridge, some over 5,000 km3. So 'city-sized blocks' is accurate and conservative. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nu%CA%BBuanu_Slide , https://www.usgs.gov/publications/giant-hawaiian-landslides , https://www.usgs.gov/publications/prodigious-submarine-landslides-hawaiian-ridge , https://usgs.gov/news/volcano-watch-oahu-niihau-and-kauai
- Mauna Kea is 4,205 m above sea level and about 6,000 m below, roughly 10,200 m from base to peak. The base definition is debated, so say 'more than 10 km'. Mauna Loa's true relief is about 17 km because the Moho is pushed down as much as 8 km. Sources: https://www.usgs.gov/faqs/how-big-are-hawaiian-volcanoes , https://usgs.gov/center-news/volcano-watch-how-high-mauna-loa
- The moat is real: the Hawaiian Deep is a flexural trough about 5.5 km deep, with an arch beyond it. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaiian_Trough
- Midway is a shield volcano about 28 million years old that sank while its reef grew upward. Drilling in 1965 (USGS) hit basalt at 157 m on Sand Island and 384 m under the reef. One 1972 K-Ar date gave 18 million years; that is an outlier, so use about 28 million years. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Midway_Atoll , https://pubs.usgs.gov/publication/70010514
- Kama'ehuakanaloa (renamed from Lo'ihi in July 2021). Summit about 975 m below sea level, last eruption probably 1996, emergence 'thousands of generations' away. Source: https://www.usgs.gov/observatories/hvo/news/volcano-watch-kamaehuakanaloa-volcano-formerly-known-loihi-seamount
- Kaga found 16-18 Oct 2019 by RV Petrel at about 5.4 km. Akagi identified 20 Oct 2019 at a similar depth. Yorktown found 19 May 1998 by Ballard at 16,650 ft (about 5 km). Nautilus filmed all three in Sept 2023. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japanese_aircraft_carrier_Kaga , https://news.mit.edu/1998/mindell-0610 , https://nautiluslive.org/blog/2023/09/14/exploring-iconic-shipwrecks-battle-midway-provide-never-seen-details , https://www.papahanaumokuakea.gov/new-news/2019/10/21/kaga/

MUST FIX:
(1) The hero shot is wrong for Kaho'olawe. At the Last Glacial Maximum (about -120 m, 18,000 years ago) only Maui, Lana'i and Moloka'i were joined. The Kaho'olawe link was 'permanently broken between 200,000 and 150,000 years ago' by subsidence (Wikipedia, Maui Nui; Star-Bulletin). Say the -120 m drop joins three islands, and let Kaho'olawe join at a deeper level that we read off the bathymetry. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maui_Nui
(2) The carriers are not 'off Midway' or on its flank. From the sinking coordinates, Kaga (30°23'N 179°17'W) is about 165 nmi (about 300 km) northwest of Midway and Yorktown (30°36'N 176°34'W) about 150 nmi north; the press said 'about 200 miles north'. All three lie on the abyssal plain about 5 km down, inside Papahanaumokuakea. Soryu and Hiryu remain unfound in every report I saw.
(3) Laupahoehoe death counts vary, so say 'more than twenty people, most of them children'.
(4) Avoid the disputed Lana'i mega-tsunami deposits and any mega-tsunami hype. USGS treats giant collapses as very rare.
(5) The 1946 wave came from Alaska and is not part of Hawaiian geology. It is a metaphor for the open, not part of the science.
(6) 'Every island becomes a Midway' needs one nuance: the island will sink and erode, and past the Darwin Point near Kure it drowns into a seamount rather than staying an atoll.

PHOTOS AND FILM:

- NASA Earth Observatory, ISS and Landsat images of the islands and Midway's reef ring (public domain).
- NOAA Papahanaumokuakea and PIFSC photos of the northwestern islands and Midway (public domain).

WHAT THE ENGINE WOULD RENDER: a water plane dropping over real 3D terrain, one reveal per step:
- -120 m: Maui, Moloka'i and Lana'i join (Kaho'olawe stays separate).
- About -1 km to -4.5 km: the Nuuanu debris field, with the Tuscaloosa block in the Manhattan comparison.
- About -5.5 km: the Big Island as one cone with the moat ring and arch, the Everest mesh beside it, and a cut-away showing the bent Moho (the 17 km reveal).
- A flyover northwest along the shrinking chain with age counters, ending at Midway's reef ring with a cut-away of the reef cap over sunken basalt.
- Zoom out to wreck markers on the flat abyssal floor about 150-165 nmi north and northwest, using simple ship meshes (no CC0 carrier models exist, so we build them).
- Swing back southeast to the Kama'ehuakanaloa cone at -975 m, then refill.

The 1946 open would need low-poly characters on a reef flat, which is tonally delicate (see red flags). The whole film keeps one photoreal-terrain look, which fixes ep01's style clash.
check.story_strength:
6/10.

CHARACTERS: The only human figures are the anonymous 1946 Laupahoehoe children and teachers in the cold open and the Midway sailors in one chapter. Zero to two named people. The real 'character' is the Big Island and its future.

STAKES: Mostly wonder, not jeopardy. There is no human goal running through the film.

TICKING CLOCK: The drain itself, an artificial but effective device. One new thing per depth step gives about 6 clear reveals, the same engine as the 1.8M Antarctica video. The islands' own sinking is too slow to feel urgent.

TWIST: The conveyor ('Midway was once a Big Island; the Big Island will be a Midway') is good but moderately well known; Signore Galilei's 3M video and the Shorts carry versions of it. The stronger, less-used twist is the moat: the mountain is so heavy it pushed the seafloor down, making Mauna Loa about 17 km tall from its true base. 'Taller than Everest' alone is spent (17M-view Shorts).

ENDING: The newborn island below the Big Island, then the refill ('everything you know is the tip'), is satisfying and loops back to the open.

PHONE GRAMMAR: Excellent. One big shape per beat, a giant water line, and a few big numbers fix ep01's tiny-label problem.

WEAKNESSES: The human spine is thin. The 1946 open and Midway are bookends around a geology tour, and the Midway chapter is a detour that only works if the carriers are framed honestly as about 150 nmi out on the abyssal plain. It makes a stronger spectacle film than story film. Its retention ceiling depends on how fast the reveals come.
check.red_flags:
1. FACT ERROR IN THE HERO SHOT: At -120 m (the Last Glacial Maximum), Kaho'olawe was not part of Maui Nui; the link broke 150,000-200,000 years ago. Only Maui, Moloka'i and Lana'i join.

2. WRECK GEOGRAPHY: Kaga, Akagi and Yorktown lie about 150-165 nmi (about 280-300 km) north and northwest of Midway on the abyssal plain, about 5 km down. They are not 'off' the atoll or on its flank. Soryu and Hiryu are unfound. Do not imply all four or five carriers are there.

3. TONE OF THE COLD OPEN: The Laupahoehoe hook uses the deaths of about 16-20 schoolchildren and their teachers. The line 'For a few minutes the sea drained away. We're going to finish the job' risks sounding glib over a child-death disaster, and it clashes with the owner's wish for funny scenes. Animating children running onto the reef needs great care. The wave also came from Alaska, so the open is a metaphor, not part of the science. If kept, treat it solemnly and briefly. An alternative is the 1975 Kalapana M7.7 quake, when Kilauea's south flank slid seaward, the coast dropped about 3.5 m and a local tsunami killed 2 campers at Halape. It ties directly to the landslide chapter. That date is from memory, so verify it.

4. TITLE COLLISION: 'What Hawaii Looks Like Without Water' is already the exact title of a 105-minute Bright Side Dark Secrets video (9K views). The Korean channel posted the exact premise 8 days ago. Choose a distinct title.

5. RACE RISK: Unseen Works (the 1.8M Antarctica channel) posted 'Pacific Drained' 4 days ago and iterates fast. A Hawaii-specific video from them is plausible soon.

6. SEARCH IS ZERO: vidIQ shows under 750 searches a month for the exact phrase. Like ep01, this lives or dies on Suggested CTR, and ep01's Suggested CTR was 1.97%.

7. NUMBERS THAT DRAW PEDANT COMMENTS: Mauna Kea's '10,000 m' depends on the base definition. Mauna Loa is bigger by volume and from its depressed base. Midway's age has an old 18-million-year outlier. Laupahoehoe death counts vary (21 to 25). Use rounded, hedged phrasing.

8. NO MEGA-TSUNAMI HYPE: Keep the USGS framing: giant flank collapses happen on time scales of about 100,000 years. Skip the disputed Lana'i 'giant wave' deposits.

9. RIGHTS: The wreck imagery (OET/NOAA models, Vulcan sonar) and most Laupahoehoe photos are not clearly public domain. Plan to render the wrecks ourselves.

10. THIN HUMAN SPINE: There are no named characters, and retention rests entirely on reveal pacing.

As pitched, the ending is a fact much of the audience already knows. The one big number that is still unclaimed is Mauna Loa at about 17 km from its depressed base (USGS). My probes found only TheGeoModels at 38K and Sunless Deep at 1.4K near it, so it has to be the climax, not a mid-film aside.

3. FACT ERROR IN THE HERO SHOT (confirmed). At the Ice Age low (about -120 m, about 18,000 years ago) only Maui, Lana'i and Moloka'i were joined, plus the now-sunken Penguin Bank. The Maui to Kaho'olawe link was 'permanently broken between 200,000 and 150,000 years ago' (Wikipedia, Maui Nui). Saying Kaho'olawe joins at 0:30 would be a false claim in the first minute.

4. WRECK GEOGRAPHY OVERSOLD. 'The carriers lying in the deep water nearby' is misleading. Great-circle distance from the sinking coordinates: Kaga (30°23'N 179°17'W) is about 306 km / 165 nmi from Midway, and Yorktown (30°36'N 176°34'W) about 277 km / 149 nmi. Both lie on the abyssal plain more than 5 km down, not on the volcano. Soryu and Hiryu have not been found in any report seen so far. So the 'battle fought on the grave of a volcano' chapter is a detour unless the distance is stated honestly.

5. COLD-OPEN TONE AND RELEVANCE. Laupahoehoe, 1 April 1946, killed 16 schoolchildren plus teachers and residents: 24 dead according to Wikipedia (16 children, 4 teachers, 4 residents), or '16 children and five teachers' according to Earth Magazine. Following child deaths with 'We're going to finish the job' is glib. It invites angry comments, sits against the owner's 'funny scenes' brief, and animating children running onto the sand is hard to do with taste. The wave also came from an Aleutian earthquake, so it has nothing to do with Hawaiian geology. It is a metaphor, not a story beat.

6. THIN HUMAN SPINE versus the 'story-driven' hard rule. As pitched there are 0-2 named people, and the film is a geology tour between two bookends. Its own check scored story strength 6/10. Unless it is reframed, it fails the spirit of 'story-driven'.

7. ABSTRACT-GEOLOGY RELAPSE. The Moho and flexure cut-away, the hotspot mechanics and the Emperor bend (about 47-50 million years ago) are the same 'abstract geology' that lost ep01's phone viewers (2:11 average on mobile). If each of these runs longer than one big visual metaphor, mobile retention repeats ep01.

8. HIDDEN SATURATION / RACE (not fatal). The exact premise exists in low-effort form: Bright Side Dark Secrets 'What Hawaii Looks Like Without Water (The 30,000 ft Drop)' (9K, 105 min, already owns the working-title words) and the Korean channel's 36-minute version (2.3K, 8 days old). Unseen Works 'What the Pacific Ocean Looks Like Drained?' has 117K in 4 days. I could not open its contents (YouTube returned 429), but it very likely shows Mauna Kea and the Hawaiian ridge as one segment, and that channel iterates fast. Below The Map 'Hawaii Is Hiding Something Nobody Talks About' has 124K in 1 month, and Geo Metrics' video with the same title has 78K. Both surface for 'hawaiian islands sinking' and 'hawaii ocean floor map'; their contents are unverified and could overlap. The Midway wrecks are heavily covered (House of History 3.18M, Nat Geo Pacific War Wrecks 2.47M, Deep Sea Relics Akagi 419K, Skynea 327K, Forgotten Fleet 142K). No well-made Hawaii-only drain exists, so the gap is real, but it is closing.
9. ZERO SEARCH. The exact phrase gets under 750 searches a month (vidIQ). The film lives or dies on Suggested CTR next to the drain cluster, and ep01's Suggested CTR was 1.97%.

10. PEDANT AND DEBATED POINTS. The '10,000 m' base definition is disputed, and Mauna Loa, not Mauna Kea, is the larger mountain and the 17 km one. Darwin's subsidence model is right that atolls sit on sunken volcanoes, but the ring shape is debated (Droxler and Jorry's antecedent-karst model has its own videos, e.g. Ifremer 'Darwin's theory of atolls formation is incorrect!'). The tsunami warning system came in 1949, not 1948. The Nu'uanu tsunami is modelled, not observed.

WHAT DID NOT LAND. Advertiser risk is low: geology, an educational WWII segment and a non-graphic historical tragedy are all ad-safe if nothing is graphic. There is more than enough true material for 13-15 minutes without padding. The drain shot is native to our engine and reads well on a phone.
verified_claims: Mauna Kea: 4,205 m above sea level and about 6,000 m below it to the deep ocean floor, 'nearly 33,500 feet (10,211 meters)' in total, 'considerably higher' than Everest. Source: USGS FAQ, https://www.usgs.gov/faqs/how-big-are-hawaiian-volcanoes

Mauna Loa: 4,170 m above sea level, flanks another 5,000 m down to the sea floor, and its mass has pushed the sea floor and Moho down by as much as 8 km. 'Total relief ... from its true base to its summit, is about 17,170 m (56,000 ft)', which is about 1.94 times Everest (8,849 m). Sources: USGS Volcano Watch, https://www.usgs.gov/center-news/volcano-watch-how-high-mauna-loa , and the USGS FAQ above ('about 17 km above its base').

Nu'uanu slide: collapse of Ko'olau volcano (O'ahu) 1 to 1.5 million years ago, about 200 km long, 'one of the largest landslides on Earth'. Blocks lie on the seafloor up to about 100 miles NE of O'ahu, and USGS says 'the largest of these blocks is about the same size as Manhattan Island'. USGS (Moore et al.) counts 68 slides longer than 20 km on the ridge, some over 200 km long and over 5,000 km3, 'believed to have produced major tsunamis'. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nu%CA%BBuanu_Slide , https://www.usgs.gov/news/volcano-watch-oahu-niihau-and-kauai , https://www.usgs.gov/publications/giant-hawaiian-landslides

Maui Nui: Maui, Lana'i and Moloka'i were joined most recently about 18,000 years ago. Kaho'olawe's link was 'permanently broken between 200,000 and 150,000 years ago'. Penguin Bank, west of Moloka'i, is a now fully drowned part of Maui Nui. At its peak about 1.2 million years ago Maui Nui covered 14,600 km2, '50% larger than today's Hawai'i Island'. The seafloor between the four islands is about 500 m deep. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maui_Nui

The moat: the Hawaiian Deep/Trough is about 5,500 m deep and caused by the islands' weight bending the lithosphere. The Hawaiian Arch rises about 200 m beyond it. Hawai'i Island is subsiding about 2.5 mm a year. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaiian_Trough

Midway: formed about 28 million years ago over the same hotspot. It was a shield volcano 'possibly about as large as Lanai' that subsided while its reef grew upward. The reef cap is more than 157 m thick on the island and 384 m in the lagoon. It lies 2,110 km NW of Honolulu at 28°12'N 177°21'W. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Midway_Atoll

Kure is the world's northernmost atoll, about 30 million years old, at the Darwin Point. North of there reef growth cannot keep up with sinking, and the atoll will join the rest of the chain as seamounts. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kure_Atoll . The Emperor chain: about 6,200 km and more than 80 volcanoes, with the bend at about 47-50 million years ago. Detroit Seamount is 81 million years old (Meiji probably older), and the chain ends at the Kuril-Kamchatka Trench. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaiian%E2%80%93Emperor_seamount_chain

Kama'ehuakanaloa (renamed from Lo'ihi in July 2021): summit 975 m below sea level, last eruption probably in 1996, and 'it will be millennia before' it emerges. Source: https://www.usgs.gov/observatories/hvo/news/volcano-watch-kamaehuakanaloa-volcano-formerly-known-loihi-seamount

Midway wrecks: Kaga sank at 30°23'N 179°17'W and was found on 18 Oct 2019 by RV Petrel, upright at about 5.4 km. Yorktown's wreck is at 30°36'N 176°34'W, found on 19 May 1998 by Ballard about 3 miles (5 km) down. Akagi was first located by the Vulcan mapping survey in 2019. Nautilus surveyed all three in Sept 2023 at depths below 5,100 m, 'within Papahanaumokuakea Marine National Monument'. My great-circle calculation puts Kaga about 306 km / 165 nmi and Yorktown about 277 km / 149 nmi from Midway. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japanese_aircraft_carrier_Kaga , https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USS_Yorktown_(CV-5) , https://nautiluslive.org/blog/2023/09/14/exploring-iconic-shipwrecks-battle-midway-provide-never-seen-details

1946 tsunami: caused by an Aleutian earthquake of about Mw 8.6 (first estimated at Ms 7.4). It reached Hilo about 4.9 hours later and killed 159 people in Hawai'i, 96 of them in Hilo. At Laupahoehoe the sea was 'sucking all the water out of the bay', children went to look at fish flopping on the sand, and 24 people died: 16 schoolchildren, 4 teachers and 4 residents (Wikipedia). Earth Magazine gives '16 children and five teachers'. The first warning system was set up in 1949. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1946_Aleutian_Islands_earthquake , https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laup%C4%81hoehoe,_Hawaii , https://www.earthmagazine.org/article/benchmarks-april-1-1946-hawaii-tsunami-ushers-pacific-wide-warning-system/

Alternative open, verified: on 29 Nov 1975 an Mw 7.7 earthquake (also listed as 7.2) sourced on the Hilina Slump killed 2 people. The south coast subsided up to 3.7 m and a tsunami reached 14 m. The detail that the two dead were campers at Halape is not on that page, so verify it. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1975_Hawaii_earthquake

Chain beats that add people to the middle, verified: Nihoa is 7.2 million years old, Native Hawaiians lived on or visited it around AD 1000 with farm terraces and house sites, and it may have supported up to about 100 people. Nihoa and Necker have unique stone platforms. At French Frigate Shoals, La Perouse Pinnacle (37 m) is 'the only remnant of its volcanic origins'. In October 2018 Hurricane Walaka 'eroded away most of East Island' (about 11 acres), and by 2024 it had recovered to about 60%. Tern Island was a WWII emergency airstrip, the 'coral carrier'. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nihoa , https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Frigate_Shoals

Darwin explained atolls as sunken volcanoes with reef caps in 1842, after the Beagle voyage. The ring shape is now debated (Droxler and Jorry, antecedent karst). Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atoll . J. Tuzo Wilson proposed the hotspot idea in 1963. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii_hotspot

Not verified, because the web-search budget ran out (WebFetch on known pages only): James G. Moore's 1964 proposal of the giant slides and their confirmation by GLORIA sonar in 1986-91; Akagi's exact coordinates; whether Soryu or Hiryu have been found as of Nov 2026; what the Unseen Works Pacific video and the Below The Map video actually contain. YouTube watch pages returned 429.
fixes: 1. MAKE IT A LIFE STORY, NOT A TOUR. The protagonist is a Hawaiian volcano, and the film follows its life: birth (Kama'ehuakanaloa), giant (Big Island), collapse (Nu'uanu), drowning (Maui Nui / Penguin Bank), skeleton (La Perouse Pinnacle), atoll (Midway), grave (Kure's Darwin Point, then the Emperor seamounts heading into the Kamchatka trench). Every chapter is one life stage, so the story has a direction and the 'story-driven' rule is met.

2. SPLIT THE TWO ENGINES SO THE SECOND HALF KEEPS ITS PULL. First half: the vertical DRAIN LADDER on the main islands (-120 m, -500 m, -2,000 m, -5,500 m), one reveal per step. Second half: a TIME MACHINE with an on-screen '+ million years' counter. Morph the Big Island mesh into each older island as it sinks and erodes (+2 Myr looks like Maui, +5 like Kaua'i, +7 like Nihoa, +28 like Midway). That replaces the flat NW flyover with a countdown and a repeating 'this is your future' reveal.

3. MOVE THE ONLY UNSPENT NUMBER TO THE CLIMAX (about 85%). After the time machine, return to the fully drained Big Island and say 'we haven't reached the bottom yet'. Then drain the rock: a cut-away shows the crust sagging up to 8 km under Mauna Loa, and the mountain's true height counts up to about 17 km, almost twice Everest (USGS). Show it as one physical metaphor (a bowling ball on a mattress). Then the coda: Kama'ehuakanaloa 975 m down, and refill. Keep 'taller than Everest' (10.2 km) as a mid-film beat only.

4. FIX THE HERO SHOT. At -120 m join only Maui, Moloka'i and Lana'i, plus Penguin Bank appearing as a lost fourth land. Bring Kaho'olawe in at the depth the HMRG/ETOPO bathymetry actually shows (the shelf between the islands is about 500 m). Optional line: Maui Nui was once 50% bigger than today's Big Island.

5. STATE THE WRECK DISTANCES HONESTLY. Draw a 280-300 km line from Midway north and northwest to the wreck markers on the abyssal plain (Kaga about 165 nmi, Yorktown about 150 nmi), and say they lie more than 5 km down, inside Papahanaumokuakea. Mention only the three surveyed wrecks, not Soryu or Hiryu. Keep the Midway battle to 60-90 seconds and use it as the human anchor of the 'atoll' stage, not a separate WWII film. Treat the wrecks as war graves: respectful, no gore. Render the ships ourselves and avoid OET/Vulcan imagery.

6. REPLACE OR REWORK THE COLD OPEN. Preferred: a funny, on-brand animated open, e.g. a low-poly tourist on Waikiki pulls a giant bathtub plug and the water line starts to drop, and the hero shot comes before 0:30. That fits the owner's 'funny scenes' brief and is safe for advertisers. If Laupahoehoe stays, move it to the Nu'uanu/tsunami chapter as a short, solemn beat with '16 schoolchildren' (the figure both sources agree on), say the wave came from Alaska, and drop 'we're going to finish the job'. The 1975 Hilina Slump quake (2 dead, coast dropped 3.7 m) is a better geological link for the landslide chapter. Verify the Halape detail first.

7. ADD NAMED PEOPLE TO THE MIDDLE, ONE BEAT EACH. Darwin (1842: atolls are sunken volcanoes; Midway's 384 m reef cap on basalt fits; mention that the ring shape is debated). The Polynesians on Nihoa around AD 1000 (farm terraces, stone platforms). The 2018 Walaka storm that washed most of East Island away, which has since come back to about 60%. Optional: James G. Moore and the 'impossible' giant landslides, only after verifying 1964 and the GLORIA confirmation with a primary USGS source.

8. SHAPE IT FOR PHONES. Give every reveal one huge shape, a giant depth counter and at most one label. Use inset zooms for small objects (the wrecks are 250 m on a 300 km frame; La Perouse Pinnacle is 37 m). Use hypsometric tint and low sun so the drained seafloor is not a grey mush. Cap the hotspot, flexure and Emperor-bend explanations at about 20 seconds of plain-language motion each. No subscribe ask mid-film; end on the refill line and hand off to the next video.

9. TITLE AND THUMBNAIL FOR SUGGESTED, NOT SEARCH. Never use 'What Hawaii Looks Like Without Water'. Lead with the unspent number, e.g. 'We Drained the Ocean Around Hawaii. The Mountain Underneath Is Almost Twice Everest' or 'Hawaii Is the Tip of a 17 km Mountain'. Hedge in the narration that this is Mauna Loa measured from its true base. Thumbnail: the half-drained Big Island with a big water line, a small Everest beside it and '17 KM' in large type, matching the grammar of the Unseen Works and Contour Atlas drain videos so it gets recommended beside them.

10. HEDGE THE NUMBERS PEDANTS WILL CHECK. Say 'more than 10 km' for Mauna Kea, 'about 17 km' for Mauna Loa from its true base, 'about 28 million years' for Midway and 'thousands of years at least' for Kama'ehuakanaloa. Say the next island could form there, not that it will on a schedule. Keep the USGS framing that giant collapses are very rare: no mega-tsunami hype and no Lana'i 'giant wave' deposits. Present the Nu'uanu tsunami as modelled, not witnessed.

11. SHIP FAST. Unseen Works (the 1.8M Antarctica channel) posted its Pacific drain 4 days ago, and a Korean channel posted the exact premise 8 days ago. Before scripting, someone with an unthrottled browser should watch the Unseen Works Pacific video and the Below The Map 'Hawaii Is Hiding Something' video, and cut any reveal they already show.

titles: 1) Hawaii Is Only the Tip. We Drained the Ocean. [45 chars] - Puts the place in word 1 and uses the drain host words (Drained, Ocean). It states a fact and holds back one thing: the tip of what? No number and no Everest. It is true: most of every Hawaiian volcano is underwater, by height and by volume. If 'only the tip' draws joke comments, use the same idea as 'Hawaii Is Only the Summit. We Drained the Ocean.' [48].

2) We Drained Hawaii's Ocean. Here's What Was Hiding. [50] - Uses the exact wording of Contour Atlas's drain titles (170K and 165K), so YouTube matches it best to those videos. The gap is generic, and Hawaii only appears at word 3.

3) Hawaii With the Ocean Drained Away [34] - Plain and descriptive, like the 1.8M 'What Antarctica Looks Like Without Ice'. It is never cut off on compact cards. It has the weakest curiosity gap, which makes it the best title to A/B test against #1.

4) Drain Hawaii's Ocean and a 6-Mile Mountain Appears [50] - Concrete and in US units, and true: Mauna Kea is more than 10 km (6.3 mi) from base to peak. But it is the worn 'taller than Everest' fact in new wording, and it copies the structure of the 8-day-old Korean exact-premise title.

5) Hawaii Without Water: The Mountain Under Paradise [49] - Contains the exact search phrase, which matters only for a small search tail. It sits close to the Bright Side Dark Secrets title, and 'paradise' is a soft word.

7) Half an Oahu Volcano Is Lying on the Seafloor [45] - True: the Nuuanu slide took about half of Ko'olau. It is the least-known fact in the film. But it sells one chapter, invites mega-tsunami expectations we will not meet, and puts 'Oahu' at word 3.

8) Hawaii Is Sinking. Midway Shows What Comes Next. [48] - True: the islands subside as they ride off the hotspot, and it carries the US and WWII anchor. pack.cold_open:
COLD OPEN, 0:00-0:30. About 78 words, roughly 30 s at Rodney's ~153 wpm. No named people, no dates, one spoken number. Sentences are 12 words or fewer. No menu.

[0:00] Frame 1 is Thumbnail 1 in motion: the same camera northeast of Hilo, with the water already sliding down the Big Island's flank. The yellow dashed SEA LEVEL line stays fixed at the old shore and is the only label, so the shot works with the sound off.
N: "This is Hawaii's Big Island. We're draining the ocean around it."

[0:04] The water keeps falling. Drowned reef steps and gullies break the surface, and the camera eases in over 1.5 s.
N: "The shore becomes a ledge. The mountain keeps going."

[0:08] The water stops at about -4,000 m. Hold 1 s on the thumbnail composition: a thin green-and-black cap above the yellow line, a giant warm-lit flank below.
N: "The Hawaii on every postcard? That's only the tip." (The title is paid off here, at about 0:10.)

[0:11] Hard cut: the sea snaps back to normal, then an eased 2-second flight northwest to Maui, Molokai and Lanai at regional zoom.
N: "Let's do it properly, one step at a time."

[0:14] A big '-400 FT' label appears. The water drops, the shallow banks surface as tan land, and the three islands fuse into one island in the accent colour. Kaho'olawe stays separate and dimmed.
N: "Drop the sea four hundred feet, and three islands become one."

[0:20] A low golden-hour pass across the new land bridge, with a few seabirds wheeling over the dry channel.
N: "That's not a what-if. In the last Ice Age, Maui, Molokai and Lanai were one island."

[0:26] The drain resumes. The camera tips over the new coast and down the slope into deep blue as the water plane slides past.
N: "That barely scratches it. Keep draining, and Hawaii stops looking like islands."

NOTES:
1. I moved the 1946 Laupahoehoe children out of the cold open, for three reasons. Opening on them delays the title payoff past 10 s. The 'finish the job' line reads as glib over the deaths of more than twenty people, most of them children. And the wave came from Alaska, so it is not part of the geology. If the writer keeps it, give it about 15 s at the start of the Big Island chapter, played solemnly, using PD Hilo photos and the real reef flat, with no animated children.
2. Check on the HMRG grid that the Maui-Molokai-Lanai saddles actually come out of the water at -120 to -130 m (about 400 ft). If they need -130 m, the narration stays correct.
3. Nothing about Everest, the moat, the landslide or Midway appears in the first 30 s. Those are the later reveals.

finalists.working_title: We Drained Lake Powell Down to Dead Pool
finalists.premise: Lake Powell, America's second-largest reservoir, hit a record low in August 2026, then jumped about 12-16 ft in October storms. We remove the rest of the water using the USGS topobathymetric model (2017 multibeam, 2018 lidar and pre-dam surveys), and the drowned Glen Canyon comes back: side canyons, the Cathedral in the Desert, stranded marinas, the power-pool and dead-pool lines, and a mud delta over 100 ft thick creeping toward the dam. The dam itself is the human story: in 1983 it nearly tore itself apart from too much water, and in 2026 it came within about 30 ft of losing power from too little.
finalists.story_spine: COLD OPEN, June 1983: the dam's spillway tunnel coughs red sandstone and concrete into the river, and crews bolt plywood, then steel boards, onto the gates to hold the lake back. 'In 1983 this lake nearly broke the dam. In 2026 it nearly ran dry.' HERO SHOT BY 0:30: the water plane drops 100 ft in one move and canyon walls appear. CH2: the canyon nobody knew before 1963 (at most 2 names: Brower, who traded it away and regretted it, and Dominy, who built the dam). CH3, drain step 1: full pool, and the 1983 cavitation crisis shown as a cut-away of the tunnel. CH4: the record low of 3,519.91 ft strands Hite Marina, and the Cathedral in the Desert re-emerges. CH5: 3,490 ft, the turbines stop; 3,370 ft, dead pool, and the river can no longer pass the dam. TWIST (about 85% in): the lake is filling from the bottom, with sediment deltas taking roughly 7% of capacity since 1963, and the October flood brought more. PAYOFF: the full drain down to the mud and bedrock, the dam standing in front of a canyon it can no longer fill. One-sentence answer: under Lake Powell is a drowned canyon, and the lake is slowly turning into mud. Hand-off: Lake Peigneur.

check.facts_status:
The core story is true and well documented. Several premise details need correcting or softer wording.

TRUE:
1. Lake Powell is the second-largest US reservoir. The AP record-low story says so: https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/lake-powell-hits-record-low-threatening-key-water-and-electricity-supply-for-millions

2. Record low: CORRECT THE NUMBER.
   - 3,519.91 ft was only the provisional mid-August 2026 reading, 0.01 ft under the April 2023 record.
   - The lake kept falling. NASA Earth Observatory gives 3,517.24 ft on Sept 10, 2026: https://science.nasa.gov/earth/earth-observatory/lake-powell-drops-to-record-low-levels/
   - The low was 3,516.62 ft in mid-September 2026: https://earthsky.org/earth/lake-powell-is-shrinking-dead-pool-2026/ and https://www.worldatlas.com/lakes/lake-mead-lost-192-feet-lake-powell-lost-179.html
   - Confirm with Reclamation daily data before scripting.

3. 'Within about 30 ft of losing power': true. 3,516.6 minus 3,490 is about 27 ft.

4. Minimum power pool 3,490 ft and dead pool 3,370 ft:
   - https://www.grandcanyontrust.org/blog/how-glen-canyon-dam-works
   - Reclamation's 2024 memo treats about 3,394 ft as a practical outlet floor, and flags cavitation and scour risk if water has to leave only through the four bypass tubes: https://www.usbr.gov/uc/DocLibrary/Memos/20240326-EstablishmentInterimOperatingGuidanceGlenCanyonDamLowReservoirLevels-TechnicalDecisionMemo-508-TSC.pdf

5. The October 2026 jump: true, but figures vary.
   - KSL: more than 10 ft in the month, about 3,532 ft: https://www.ksl.com/article/51641721/lake-powell-gained-more-than-10-feet-this-month-will-its-run-continue
   - KJZZ: about 14 ft; about 850K acre-feet of rain-driven inflow; it would take about 5 straight good winters to reach half full: https://www.kjzz.org/science/2026-11-04/recent-rains-were-a-drop-in-the-bucket-for-colorado-river-reservoir-water
   - Fox 10 reports a 16-ft surge.
   - Inflow of 65,000 cfs was the second-highest October daily inflow since 1963.
   - Say 'about 15 feet' and date-stamp it.

6. 1983: well documented.
   - The left spillway opened June 2. On June 6 there was rumbling and material was thrown out of the tunnel exit.
   - The water was tinted red by eroded Navajo sandstone (PopSci: https://www.popsci.com/scitech/article/2003-03/water-vapor-almost-busts-dam).
   - The crater in the tunnel was 32 ft deep, 40 ft wide and 150-180 ft long (sources differ).
   - Flashboards were 4-ft plywood, then 8-ft steel boards in early July.
   - The peak was 3,708.34 ft in mid-July 1983, 6.6 ft below the dam crest:
     - https://damfailures.org/case-study/glen-canyon-dam-arizona-1983
     - https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Risks_to_the_Glen_Canyon_Dam
     - https://coyotegulch.blog/2019/07/19/for-a-while-in-1983-sheets-of-plywood-were-all-that-kept-the-mighty-glen-canyon-dam-from-overflowing-arizona-central/
   - SOFTEN the wording. It was the spillway tunnels that were tearing apart. Engineers feared losing control and damage reaching the rock, but the concrete dam itself was not observed failing. Use 'the spillways were tearing themselves apart' and 'within 7 ft of the top', not 'the lake nearly broke the dam'.

7. Brower traded Glen Canyon to stop Echo Park Dam and later called it his great regret ('we never should have lost Glen Canyon'): true and well sourced, e.g. https://www.intermountainhistories.org/items/show/56. I could not verify the exact quote 'Glen Canyon died in 1963'; do not use it. Dominy was Reclamation Commissioner from 1959 to 1969 and championed the dam. A strong true scene: Brower and Dominy rafted the Grand Canyon together in John McPhee's 'Encounters with the Archdruid'.

8. Sediment:
   - USGS SIR 2022-5017: storage capacity fell 6.79% (1.833M acre-feet) from 1963 to 2018, about 33,270 acre-feet per year: https://pubs.usgs.gov/publication/sir20225017
   - Delta thickness: about 180 ft for the Colorado and about 120 ft for the San Juan per KNAU 2013 (https://www.knau.org/earth-notes/2013-05-08/earth-notes-glen-canyon-dam-what-flows-in-and-not-out), and about 150 ft at Hite per NPS (https://www.nps.gov/glca/learn/nature/sedimentation.htm). 'Over 100 ft' is safe.
   - SENSATIONAL RISK: 'creeping toward the dam'. The Colorado delta is more than 125 miles from the dam, and the San Juan delta is about 27 miles from the confluence (SLTrib 2022). Time to reach the dam is disputed: 80-100 years (advocates) versus 500-700 years (agencies). USGS's first-order estimate is about 750 years to fill the remaining volume. The twist is true only on a centuries timescale and must say so.

9. Hite Marina: WRONG CAUSATION in the story spine. Hite has been closed for about two decades (low water plus sediment). The 2026 low did not strand it. For 2026, use Bullfrog Marina being moved toward the main channel and the Bullfrog-Halls Crossing ferry not running: https://www.kunc.org/news/2026-05-17/its-a-different-lake-now-as-lake-powell-drops-an-iconic-marina-chases-deeper-water

10. Cathedral in the Desert re-emerged again in 2026, now with graffiti (SLTrib spring 2026). True.

11. The USGS model exists and is public domain: 1-m 'Topobathymetric DEM of Lake Powell, 1947-2018' (Danielson, Tyler, Poppenga 2020, DOI 10.5066/P9XX0J1Y; https://www.usgs.gov/data/one-meter-topobathymetric-digital-elevation-model-lake-powell-arizona-utah-1947-2018), plus a modified version by Jones and Root, 2021 (DOI 10.5066/P9H60YCF).

DO NOT SAY:
- 'nearly broke the dam'
- 'mud is about to reach the dam'
- 'biggest rise since 1964'. That is an AI-channel claim; the documented fact is the second-highest October daily inflow since 1963.

Present-tense numbers change daily, so date-stamp them.

6.5/10. It is very strong as visual spectacle and only moderate as a human story.

STRENGTHS:
- The drain ladder gives 5-7 true, escalating, phone-readable reveals: full pool, the 1983 peak, the record low, the turbines stopping, dead pool, the riverbed.
- 'Too much water in 1983, too little in 2026' is a clean, true bookend.
- The one-sentence answer works.
- There is a real ticking clock (the dropping water line toward 3,490 and 3,370; the rising one toward the crest in 1983).
- There is a vivid, true scene: plywood nailed onto a 710-ft dam, and red sandstone-tinted water.
- Brower vs Dominy is a genuine pair of rivals. Their rafting trip in McPhee's book is a usable true scene.

WEAKNESSES:
- The protagonist is a dam. The 1983 operators are mostly unnamed.
- The 2026 near-miss is an anticlimax: it never reached power pool, and then storms raised it.
- The 1983 crisis is already well told (The Hydraulic Record 171K, a 1.5M Short).
- The sediment twist is true but slow. It is centuries away and the deltas are more than 125 miles from the dam, so it lands as a reflective 'huh', not a shock.
- The payoff (a canyon under the lake) is already familiar to this audience from hundreds of drone and before/after Shorts (5.5M, 4.9M, 4.7M).

The ending ('a dam in front of a canyon it can no longer fill') is good but quiet. It would need a sharper closing image or a data hook, such as 'the lake has lost about 7% of its space to mud', to land.

kill_shots: VERDICT: it survives, but only as a reworked film. As pitched, it has a weak middle and a payoff viewers have already seen. Each problem below has a fix in 'fixes'. None of them alone kills the topic.

Template race: the 'We Drained X. Here's What Was Hidden at the Bottom.' title is being cloned within days, and views drop with each copy. My probe found Contour Atlas Chesapeake 170K, Great Lakes 165K and Tahoe 110K in 5 days. The Hidden Provinces put out Ontario 133K, Erie 72K, Georgian Bay 23K and Strait of Georgia 10K within 5 days. Then Sydney Harbour 41K, North Sea 14K, Mississippi 10K and Loch Ness 1.4K.
